title: Research Bite #85: Considering Cognitive Load When Exploring Before Instruction
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton breaks down a DeCaro et al. study on whether students should explore a problem before being taught. Across three studies with first-year engineering students learning Python errors, exploring first hurt learning when one activity bundled three ideas. When the same content was split into three short explore-then-teach cycles, exploring first improved conceptual understanding. Barton reads this through element interactivity, the number of connected ideas a learner must hold at once. He then turns it into classroom advice: target one new idea per task, build short cycles, give a precise goal, check with why questions, and do not mistake a lively room for learning. He closes with caveats on small effects, non-random semester comparisons and the university context.
points: Exploring before instruction helped understanding only when each activity targeted a single new idea; bundling three ideas into one activity reduced learning.
Splitting the same content into short explore-then-explain cycles took about the same total time, so the change is one of lesson arrangement, not extra time.
Exploration tasks need a precise goal, such as producing a specific error or finding two fractions that sum to more than 1, rather than an open instruction to explore.
Students found the complex activity more interesting yet learned less, so engagement is not evidence of learning and a short why-question check is needed.
Effect sizes were small, the comparison across versions was not a true experiment, and the sample was university engineers, so transfer to schools is uncertain.
quotes: If you start with a problem, make sure it targets one new idea. When students explored all three error types in a single activity, they scored lower than students who were taught first.
Before you open a lesson with a problem, count the new ideas a student would need to make sense of it. If there is more than one, split the task.
Plan two or three mini-cycles, each with its own brief exploration and its own brief explanation, instead of one long investigation followed by one long input.
When you set an exploration task, give a precise goal, such as “find two fractions that add to more than 1, and write down what you notice about them”, rather than “explore adding fractions”.
If you only check with quick-fire recall, you may miss the benefit. Finish each cycle with a question that asks students to explain why something happens, not just to name it.
A buzzing exploration phase tells you students are engaged. A short check of understanding at the end tells you whether they learned.
Exploring a problem before being taught helped understanding when each activity focused on one idea. When students explored three related ideas at once, they learned less than students taught first.
